t: You Actually Can, and Should, Shut if Off
q: I think there are a lot of problems with this sentiment, which you can find easily enough on teacher message boards and blogs, or in motivational keynotes for teachers, or conference sessions, or books. The problem isn’t small, either. Basically, I think this idea of being unable to turn teaching off is a recipe for being a mediocre (and unhappy) teacher and person.

And so it turns out that the best way to be the best teacher you’re capable of being is to, indeed, turn it off. If you’re like me, you love your students. So: learn to turn it off. Engage in leisure. Find purpose beyond the classroom.

Not turning teaching off doesn’t just affect our performance — it affects our quality of life, too. That’s the double whammy of the Yerkes-Dodson curve — you don’t just perform worse when you’re overly stressed; you tend to hate your life, too. Lose-lose.

But this enmeshment of my identity with my work as a teacher produces deadly consequences down the line. When I fail at something — say a lesson goes badly, or fourth hour has been hard for me to manage, or a parent complains about me to the principal — I’ll take it all the way into my heart.

But success will ruin me, too. A good assessment outcome or winning a teacher award or getting praised at the staff meeting will puff me up, making me think I’m more important than I am. This will make me insufferable to be around, and I’ll find down the line that I’ve got less friends and a slippery grip on reality.

I know that a lot of these points link back to performance, too, but I guess that’s a central part of my strategy for teaching as best I can for as long as possible: the internal work enables the external work. It’s the engine beneath the hood of the car.

Stop telling yourself that you can’t turn the work off. It’s not a good way to serve the kids that you love so much. We’ve got to think harder, for the sake of our kids and for ourselves and for the people in our lives outside of education who we love and owe our lives to.
x: Leisure and unconscious processing are not slacking but part of how hard teaching problems get solved.
Leisure and unconscious processing are not slacking but part of how hard teaching problems get solved.
Dave Stuart Jr. takes on the common claim that teaching is a calling you can never turn off, arguing that the belief makes teachers worse and unhappier.
Leisure and unconscious processing are not slacking but part of how hard teaching problems get solved.
Constant engagement with teaching stress exceeds the pressure that supports good performance, so switching off improves the work itself.
His strategy is that the internal work of detaching and recovering powers the external work of teaching.
He ends by urging teachers to stop telling themselves they cannot switch off, for the sake of students and the people at home.

q: Overwhelmingly, they suggest that long-term student flourishing comes not primarily from academic mastery, but from noncognitive factors. Today, I'd like to focus not on noncognitive factors, but on the thought experiment itself.

It’d be easy to sit there, listen to me explain the thought experiment, and say, “Well, okay. Nice parlor trick, but that’s not rigorous science. It’s just a bunch of people and their random intuition.
That’s good pushback. I want more teachers to think harder about research; this would help to reduce how the phrase “research-based” is used too lightly in education today.

In 2006, Dutch researchers Ap Dijksterhuis & Loran F. Nordgren proposed UTT in an article for Science. The researchers hypothesized that it’s not always advantageous to use “conscious deliberation” in decision-making. (They tested the hypothesis using various experiments [1].) Some decisions, they argued — particularly those with lots of variables, especially conflicting ones — are actually best left to the unconscious mind.

It’s one more reason to leave work at work. When I’m “distracted” (to use Dijksterhuis and Nordgren’s language) with non-teaching things like husbanding and fathering, I get to use UTT to wrestle with the problems facing me in the classroom. - It’s support for the teacher meetings practice of “walk away questions.” This is language we use in my district. It helps meetings stay focused on the problems at hand (i.e., problems best handled via conscious thought).

After reading the information, participants were placed into three groups: one group had to immediately decide which apartment was best; another was given time to consciously think it through and decide; and the third was given a game to play to distract them from consciously thinking about the apartment decision, thereby enabling only unconscious thought. The results? Immediate choosers and conscious thinkers didn't accurately identify the best choice apartment — only the unconscious thinkers did.
x: Stuart uses a thought experiment he runs with teachers, asking them to name the first student and descriptor that come to mind, to argue that teacher intuition deserves more respect than a sceptic might grant.
The post defends gut-level teacher judgment by linking an informal thought experiment to a specific peer-reviewed theory, rather than just asserting that intuition matters.
He anticipates the objection that this is not rigorous science and concedes that teachers should think harder about research before calling things research-based.
Unconscious Thought Theory says decisions with many conflicting variables can be better handled unconsciously, which Newport illustrates as a home computer versus Google's data centres.
The classroom takeaways are practical: leave work at work so the mind can keep processing, use 'walk away questions' in meetings, and sleep on hard problems.
The apartment-choice study, where only distracted participants picked the best flat out of 48 pieces of information, shows the effect rather than just naming it.

t: How To Handle Students Who Question Your Classroom Management nagement/
q: So when a student questions the way you manage your classroom—most often in front of the class—it can be hard not to take it personally. It can be hard not to bristle and become defensive.
Because showing frustration puts you at odds with not only the student who asked the question but with your entire class.
You calmly, even cheerfully, say your line and then move on. There is no reason to wait for a response or gird yourself for an argument.
If you can’t point to a logical reason why you have certain rules, procedures, routines, etc., then you’re asking for trouble. Because arbitrary or unexplained regulation causes resentment.
In my role coaching teachers , I find myself asking frequently “Why are you doing that? What’s the purpose?” And often they can’t tell me, which means their students don’t know either.
They don’t necessarily even have to agree. They just need to know why .
x: Linsin advises teachers on responding when a student challenges a classroom rule or procedure, often in front of the whole class.
When students question a classroom rule, reacting with frustration or defensiveness creates a 'you-against-them' dynamic with the whole class.
The recommended response is to answer calmly and cheerfully with a brief, prepared explanation and then move on without waiting for a rebuttal.
He stresses that every rule, procedure, and routine needs a clear, logical purpose that a teacher can articulate in a sentence or two; unexplained or arbitrary expectations breed resentment.
In coaching sessions, Linsin often finds teachers cannot explain the purpose behind their own practices, meaning their students don't know it either.
Linsin advises teachers on responding when a student challenges a classroom rule or procedure, often in front of the whole class.

q: There are teachers who seem blessed with natural charisma. The lucky ones.
Whatever the reason, they become almost entirely stripped of their true personality.
This is a big problem. Because when you inhabit a teaching persona that is different from your natural self, you become uninteresting and hard for students to pay attention to.

The truth is, you are charismatic. Just as you are . In fact, it’s your uniqueness, your quirks and idiosyncrasies, your vulnerability and eccentricity, even your perceived weaknesses that are your greatest strengths.
I’m nothing special. I’m introverted by nature. I’m not a smooth talker. I’m frequently awkward. Again, doesn’t matter. In fact, these very things help endear me to my students.
Charisma is nothing more than the inward acceptance and outward expression of the best of who you really are.
x: Linsin explores why some teachers seem naturally charismatic and argues the difference is not innate talent but a single behavior.
Linsin explores why some teachers seem naturally charismatic and argues the difference is not innate talent but a single behavior: embracing one's authentic self in the classroom.
Many teachers strip away their real personality out of fear or the belief that good teaching requires a buttoned-up persona, making them uninteresting to students.
A teacher's quirks, vulnerabilities, and perceived weaknesses are described as their greatest strengths for building charisma.
Linsin counters the common excuse that charisma requires natural talent by describing himself as introverted, awkward, and unpolished, yet effective.
Linsin explores why some teachers seem naturally charismatic and argues the difference is not innate talent but a single behavior: embracing one's authentic self in the classroom.

t: Improving Student Motivation via Micro-Commenting on Papers
q: I've written and spoken passionately about the need for us to think better about grading and feedback. When feedback isn't fast, it's a triple loss.
None of that's to make us feel guilty. To paraphrase The Godfather, it's not personal — it's only business. We just take a step back and say, “All right — then how do I do feedback quickly?
Isn't this way of thinking about feedback and grading a bit ruthless and utilitarian? Does it dehumanize the process, turning us into an army of robotic, cold, calculating graders?

As our colleague Matthew Johnson in Ann Arbor, MI has argued, the notes we put in the margins of kids' work are relationship-building. Often times, for those of us with 100+ kids on the roster, margin notes are a primary means through which we build relationships.
It doesn't take paragraphs to do this — on a recent pile of student work, I averaged 20-40 words per paper — but the words I use obviously matter.

My classes are not very differentiated in the sense of lots of student choice and individualized learning tasks. Part of that's a time issue on my end, but a bigger part is that it doesn't seem to be the most important way to differentiate for young people. The place to differentiate is in how we seek to help each child believe the five key things. I love that about the beliefs — they are things that all of us need in order to be motivated to do something, but they are also not things that we all arrive at along the same paths.

So no, I don't dehumanize my work with kids, even the work of grading and feedback. It's possible to do this work at a deeply human and loving level without letting a stack of papers languish in your work bag for weeks. The first step to getting there, of course, is to believe that it can be done.
x: Stuart extends his argument for fast feedback by answering a charge that quick grading is ruthless and dehumanising.
Stuart extends his argument for fast feedback by answering a charge that quick grading is ruthless and dehumanising.
Stuart extends his argument for fast feedback by answering a charge that quick grading is ruthless and dehumanising.
He answers the charge that speedy grading is cold by treating margin notes as a primary relationship-building channel when a teacher has 100-plus students.
The sample comments, grouped by crushed it, trending well, struggled and worrying, show how a 20 to 40 word note can change tone and next step by student need.
He argues the place to differentiate is in how each child comes to believe the five key things, not in individualised tasks, which his time does not allow.
The piece concludes that differentiation should happen at the level of belief-building and that grading can be both quick and loving if a teacher first believes it can be done.

t: A Little-Known Secret To Effective Teaching
q: The split second you recognize your students doing what you want or asked of them, you clam up and allow them to experience success all on their own.

Using no sudden movements, slowly ease back and away from your class. Once you reach a distance from which you can observe every student, stay silent and in one place until the task is either finished or no longer successful.
You must never send your students off on their own unless they’ve proven to you that they know what is expected.
The reason the strategy is so effective is that whenever students experience success without interference, they gain deep confidence in themselves and their own abilities.
We’ve become conditioned to always be “teaching.” We’ve been brainwashed by the powers that be into believing that good teaching looks busy.
But to make this potentially game-changing strategy work, you must purge yourself from this falsehood.
x: The core strategy: the moment students begin doing exactly what was asked, the teacher should go quiet and physically withdraw from the situation.
Teachers who habitually narrate, interrupt, and add their own commentary will find the discipline to stay silent especially difficult but essential.
The rationale is that unassisted success builds deep self-confidence and lets students enter a 'flow state' where the fastest growth and improvement occur.
Unassisted success is said to build deep self-confidence and give students room to enter a highly productive 'flow state.'.
The approach runs counter to the common belief that good teaching must always look active and busy.
The rationale is that unassisted success builds deep self-confidence and lets students enter a 'flow state' where the fastest growth and improvement occur.
